title: Technical Test 2 — Mechanical
blurb: Priority area. Heat transfer, the refrigeration cycle, chilled water plants, CRAH/CRAC, airflow, controls and response.

questions.q: Why does a data center need cooling at all?
choices: Electronics require a narrow humidity band more than a temperature band
Essentially every watt a server consumes becomes heat — a megawatt of IT load produces a megawatt of heat that must be removed
Cooling is primarily for the battery plant and switchgear rooms
To maintain positive building pressure against outside contaminants
questions.why: Heat load tracks IT load almost one-for-one. That framing is the cleanest way to open a mechanical answer.

questions.q: Which mode of heat transfer dominates in a data center?
choices: Conduction
Convection — air and water moving heat
Radiation
Evaporation, which is a fourth mode
questions.why: The three modes are conduction (solid contact), convection (moving fluid) and radiation (emitted energy).

questions.q: A ton of cooling equals:
choices: 1,000 BTU per hour
3,412 BTU per hour
12,000 BTU per hour, from the heat absorbed melting one ton of ice in 24 hours
100,000 BTU per hour
questions.why: A BTU is the heat needed to raise one pound of water one degree Fahrenheit.

questions.q: Sensible versus latent heat:
choices: Sensible changes temperature and is measurable with a thermometer; latent changes state without changing temperature
Sensible changes state; latent changes temperature
Sensible applies to air, latent applies to water
They are the same quantity measured in different units
questions.why: Latent heat is central to refrigeration — a liquid absorbs a lot of heat evaporating and releases it condensing.

questions.q: A low delta-T across a cooling coil most likely indicates:
choices: Excess cooling capacity
Poor heat transfer — fouled coil, low airflow, bypass air, or a valve not opening
The chilled water setpoint is too low
Refrigerant overcharge
questions.why: Delta-T is the difference between entering and leaving temperature. Low delta-T is a classic diagnostic flag.

questions.q: The four main components in order are:
choices: Evaporator, compressor, expansion valve, condenser
Compressor, condenser, expansion valve, evaporator
Condenser, compressor, evaporator, expansion valve
Compressor, evaporator, condenser, expansion valve
questions.why: Then back to the compressor. Memorize the order — it anchors every follow-up question.

questions.q: What does the compressor do?
choices: Drops pressure sharply to produce a cold liquid
Raises refrigerant pressure and temperature — low-pressure gas in, high-pressure hot gas out
Rejects heat to air or water
Absorbs heat from the air being cooled
questions.why: It's the pump that drives the whole cycle.

questions.q: What happens in the evaporator?
choices: Hot high-pressure gas rejects heat and condenses to liquid
Cold low-pressure refrigerant absorbs heat and boils back to gas
Liquid refrigerant is cooled below its condensing temperature
Pressure drops suddenly, dropping temperature
questions.why: The condenser rejects heat; the expansion valve drops pressure; the evaporator absorbs heat.

questions.q: Why is superheat monitored?
choices: To confirm the condenser is rejecting enough heat
To ensure only gas reaches the compressor — liquid entering a compressor causes serious damage
To verify the expansion valve is fully closed
To measure the efficiency of the cooling tower
questions.why: Subcooling is the mirror check: ensuring solid liquid, not a gas/liquid mix, reaches the expansion valve.

questions.q: Low suction pressure with high superheat suggests:
choices: Overcharge or a flooded evaporator
Insufficient refrigerant reaching the evaporator — low charge, a restriction, a starving expansion valve, or a plugged filter drier
Poor condenser heat rejection
A failed compressor unloader
questions.why: The evaporator is being starved. High head pressure is the opposite-end symptom set.

questions.q: High head pressure is most likely caused by:
choices: Low refrigerant charge
Poor heat rejection at the condenser — fouled coil, failed condenser fan, high ambient, non-condensables, or overcharge
A restriction in the liquid line
Excessive superheat at the compressor inlet
questions.why: Head pressure is a condenser-side symptom.

questions.q: Why is a refrigerant leak a compliance issue, not just a performance one?
choices: Refrigerants are regulated — leaks must be found, repaired and documented rather than just topped off
Leaks void the equipment warranty
Refrigerant is classified as a hazardous waste requiring a fire watch
It triggers an automatic impairment form
questions.why: Performance also drops as charge falls, but the reporting obligation is the part candidates forget.

questions.q: Which correctly describes the chilled water path?
choices: Chilled water runs from the cooling tower directly to the CRAH coils
Servers heat air → CRAH coil transfers that heat to chilled water → chiller pulls heat out → condenser water loop carries it to the cooling tower → atmosphere
The condenser loop runs inside the building and the chilled water loop runs outside
Chilled water is evaporated at the CRAH and condensed at the chiller
questions.why: Chilled water loop = chiller to CRAH coils inside. Condenser water loop = chiller to cooling tower.

questions.q: How does a cooling tower actually reject heat?
choices: By conduction through finned tube bundles
By evaporation — warm condenser water is sprayed over fill while air moves through, and evaporating a portion carries heat away
By mechanical refrigeration in a secondary circuit
By radiating heat to the night sky
questions.why: That's why wet bulb, not dry bulb, sets the tower's performance limit.

questions.q: Approach temperature on a cooling tower is:
choices: The difference between entering and leaving water temperature
The difference between leaving water temperature and ambient wet bulb — a rising approach indicates fouling, scaling, poor airflow or degraded fill
The difference between wet bulb and dry bulb
The setpoint minus the deadband
questions.why: A tower can never cool below wet bulb, so approach is the honest efficiency measure.

questions.q: Drift, blowdown and makeup are, respectively:
choices: Evaporated water, treated water, and recirculated water
Water carried out as droplets; water deliberately discharged to control mineral concentration; water replacing all losses
Water lost to leaks; water added for pH control; water in the sump
Airflow bypass; chemical dosing; sump level control
questions.why: Evaporation concentrates minerals, which is why blowdown exists.

questions.q: Why is condenser water treatment necessary?
choices: To prevent refrigerant contamination in the chiller barrel
Evaporation concentrates minerals causing scale and corrosion, and warm water grows biological fouling including Legionella
To raise the water's specific heat capacity
To keep the water from freezing in winter operation
questions.why: Scale, corrosion and biological growth — treatment controls all three.

questions.q: What is a plate-and-frame heat exchanger typically used for in a chilled water plant?
choices: Separating refrigerant from oil in the compressor circuit
Transferring heat between two loops without mixing them — commonly to enable water-side free cooling and idle the chillers
Pre-heating makeup water before it enters the tower
Removing non-condensables from the condenser
questions.why: It's what lets the tower cool the chilled water loop directly when it's cold enough outside.

questions.q: Cavitation in a pump is:
choices: Air entrained in the discharge line causing vibration
Vapor bubbles forming at the inlet from low pressure and collapsing violently — it damages the impeller and sounds like gravel
Impeller wear from suspended solids in the water
Overheating from running against a closed discharge valve
questions.why: The gravel sound is the classic field tell.

questions.q: The difference between a CRAH and a CRAC is:
choices: A CRAH has its own compressor; a CRAC uses chilled water
A CRAH uses chilled water from a central plant with a coil and fan only; a CRAC has its own refrigerant compressor (direct expansion, self-contained)
A CRAH serves the whole building; a CRAC serves one row
They are regional names for the same equipment
questions.why: H = handler (water). C = conditioner (its own DX circuit).

questions.q: Main components of a CRAH:
choices: Compressor, condenser, expansion valve, evaporator
Fans, a chilled water coil, a control valve modulating water flow, filters, and controls with temperature and humidity sensing
Cooling tower, pump, and heat exchanger
Damper, economizer hood, and a DX coil
questions.why: No compressor in a CRAH — the refrigeration happens at the central chiller.

questions.q: Why do data centers want high sensible cooling and little dehumidification?
choices: Dry air improves server heat transfer
The heat load is almost entirely sensible dry heat from electronics — removing moisture wastes energy and then requires humidification to add it back
Dehumidification raises the dew point
Low humidity reduces the risk of condensation on coils
questions.why: It's a pure waste loop: dehumidify then re-humidify.

questions.q: What is bypass air?
choices: Hot exhaust air looping back to a server intake
Cold supply air that returns to the cooling unit without ever passing through equipment — wasted cooling
Outside air introduced during economizer mode
Air that leaks around a closed containment door
questions.why: Recirculation is the opposite failure: hot exhaust reaching an intake and raising intake temperatures.

questions.q: What goes wrong when hot and cold air mix?
choices: Coil frost forms at the CRAH
You cool air that's already cold, waste energy and raise PUE — and server intakes can run hot even though the room average looks fine
Humidity control becomes impossible
Static pressure in the plenum drops below setpoint
questions.why: That's the whole argument for hot aisle / cold aisle containment.

questions.q: Blanking panels do what?
choices: Seal cable cutouts in the raised floor
Fill empty rack slots so hot exhaust air can't travel back through the gap to the cold side
Direct supply air upward from perforated tiles
Provide EMI shielding between racks
questions.why: Cheap and highly effective — a good example to cite when asked about low-cost wins.

questions.q: A perforated tile placed in a hot aisle:
choices: Improves return air temperature to the CRAH
Wastes cooling by delivering cold supply air where it isn't needed
Balances static pressure across the plenum
Is standard practice for containment designs
questions.why: Tile placement matters. Perf tiles belong in cold aisles.

questions.q: Why does dew point matter in a data center?
choices: It determines the maximum achievable cooling tower performance
It's the temperature at which moisture condenses out of air — condensation on energized equipment causes faults and corrosion
It sets the minimum chilled water supply temperature by code
It is the same as relative humidity expressed in degrees
questions.why: Relative humidity is moisture as a percentage of what the air could hold at that temperature, and it shifts with temperature even when moisture content doesn't.

questions.q: Humidity too low versus too high:
choices: Too low risks condensation; too high risks static discharge
Too low risks electrostatic discharge damaging electronics; too high risks condensation, corrosion and conductive contamination
Too low reduces cooling capacity; too high increases it
Neither matters if temperature is within ASHRAE limits
questions.why: ASHRAE publishes the recommended and allowable temperature and humidity envelopes you're maintaining.

questions.q: Why measure at the server intake rather than room average?
choices: Intake sensors are more accurate than room sensors
The intake is what the equipment actually experiences — room average can look fine while individual intakes run hot from recirculation or poor airflow
Room average readings are not trended in the BMS
ASHRAE specifies return-air measurement only
questions.why: This distinction is a strong thing to volunteer in an interview.

questions.q: Air-side versus water-side economization:
choices: Air-side uses a heat exchanger; water-side brings in outside air
Air-side brings filtered outside air directly into the space; water-side uses a heat exchanger so the tower cools the chilled water loop without running chillers
Both require the chillers to run at reduced capacity
Water-side is only usable below freezing
questions.why: Both are free cooling — the difference is which loop the outside conditions act on.

questions.q: How does cooling strategy trade PUE against WUE?
choices: Improving one always improves the other
Evaporative cooling lowers electrical energy for cooling (lower PUE) but consumes water (higher WUE); air-cooled chillers do the opposite
WUE only applies to air-cooled plants
PUE and WUE are unrelated metrics
questions.why: Naming it as a genuine engineering tradeoff rather than a free win is what scores.

questions.q: Why does trending matter more than a spot reading?
choices: Trends are required for PUE reporting
A single reading shows the state now; a trend shows a bearing slowly heating or an approach temperature creeping up — catching failure before it happens
Spot readings can't be logged in the BMS
Trending eliminates the need for physical rounds
questions.why: Predictive versus reactive. Good answer for a Dive Deep follow-up too.

questions.q: A deadband is:
choices: The target value the control system drives toward
The range around setpoint where no control action is taken, preventing constant cycling on small deviations
The range outside which an alarm is generated
The delay before a piece of equipment is allowed to restart
questions.why: The setpoint is the target; the deadband is the tolerance around it.

questions.q: Short cycling is damaging because:
choices: It gradually lowers refrigerant charge
Frequent starting and stopping causes excessive wear, high inrush and poor efficiency — usually from an oversized unit or bad control setting
It raises the wet bulb temperature at the tower
It causes the VFD to trip on overfrequency
questions.why: Diagnosing it as a sizing or control problem, not an equipment fault, is the useful instinct.

questions.q: Why is filter changing more important than it sounds?
choices: Dirty filters release particulates onto server intakes
A loaded filter restricts airflow, reducing cooling capacity and forcing fans to work harder — simple work with outsized consequence
Filters are the primary humidity control element in a CRAH
Filter changes are required to close out impairment forms
questions.why: Typical CRAH PM: filters, coil cleaning, fan belts and bearings, condensate drain and pan, valve operation, sensor calibration, leak checks.

questions.q: Room temperature is rising but the chillers appear to be running normally. What's the strongest first move?
choices: Lower the chilled water setpoint and monitor
Verify the reading is real and not a sensor, then determine whether it's the whole room or localized — localized points to airflow, not capacity
Start the backup chiller immediately
Open all perforated tiles to increase supply airflow
questions.why: Then check CRAHs running, valves open, filters clean, chilled water temperature and flow, containment breaches, blanking panels, tile placement — and escalate early while investigating.

questions.q: What suggests an airflow problem rather than a capacity problem?
choices: Chilled water supply temperature rising above setpoint
Localized hot spots while total cooling capacity and chilled water temperatures look normal
All CRAH units running at 100% fan speed
Rising approach temperature at the cooling tower
questions.why: Capacity problems show up broadly; airflow problems show up in specific places.

questions.q: A pump is running but flow is low. What do you check?
choices: Refrigerant charge and superheat
Valve positions, strainer blockage, air in the loop, rotation direction, impeller condition, VFD speed command, and whether it's cavitating
Compressor unloader staging
Cooling tower fill condition
questions.why: Work from the cheapest and most likely outward: valves and strainers before impellers.

questions.q: Putting a system in maintenance mode before work means:
choices: Locking out all electrical energy sources to the unit
Disabling automatic responses and alarms so your work doesn't trigger a false alarm or unwanted control action — and so the facility knows the system is temporarily impaired
Switching the unit to manual fan control only
Transferring the load to the redundant unit
questions.why: It's about not creating false signals and about the facility knowing the state.

questions.q: When should you escalate a mechanical problem?
choices: Only after exhausting your own troubleshooting steps
Early — in a critical facility the cost of downtime far exceeds the cost of asking for help; escalate while continuing to work the problem
When the customer reports an outage
Once the BMS generates a critical alarm
questions.why: Escalating early and continuing to work is the answer that shows judgment rather than ego.

questions.q: You're facing mechanical equipment you've never seen before. Best approach?
choices: Trace the piping and start with the most accessible component
Find the documentation and sequence of operation, understand what the system is trying to do, ask someone who knows it, and verify current state before changing anything
Put it in maintenance mode and begin standard PM
Wait for a specialist contractor before touching anything
questions.why: This is also the strongest honest answer when a mechanical question exceeds your field experience.
